results.text:
With one pool per state, no variance estimate and no valid p-value are possible. I'll rank the features by fold change and say so.
Fifteen of the 300 features are higher in the fasted pool than in the fed pool, but none of them is statistically tested. There is only one pooled sample per state, so there is no variance to test against. I ranked features by fold change instead of reporting p-values.

- **Result:** All 15 have a log2 fold change (fasted/fed) of at least 1. All 15 are higher in fasted, with log2 fold changes up to 1.74 (about 3.3-fold). The first rows, M6, M4, M5, M12 and M14, have the largest changes. `output/differing_features.csv` lists them.
- **Everything else:** The other 285 features have a log2 fold change of exactly 0. Their intensities are identical in the two pools. That is unusual for real LC-MS data. It suggests the table was normalized, gap-filled or simulated in a way that flattens most features. No feature is higher in fed.
- **Threshold:** The |log2 fold change| ≥ 1 cutoff is my own choice, not a statistical criterion. None of the 15 features sits at the 50,000 intensity floor, so gap-filled values are not driving the changes.
- **Not done:** The `pvalue` and `adjusted_pvalue` columns are left empty. I did no annotation, no pathway analysis and no figures. Pooling also hides differences between animals. Treat the 15 as candidates to check in individual-animal samples, not as confirmed differences.

Files are in `/analysis-001/runs/run-001/T1S1`:

m <- read.csv("/analysis-001/data/inputs/f-meta/samples.csv")
X <- as.matrix(d[, m$sample]); X[X <= 0] <- NA
rownames(X) <- d$protein_id
L <- log2(X)
grp <- m$genotype
# missingness summary + filter: >=70% detected in at least one group
det <- sapply(unique(grp), function(g) rowMeans(!is.na(L[, grp == g, drop=FALSE])))
keep <- apply(det, 1, max) >= 0.7
cat("proteins:", nrow(L), "kept:", sum(keep), "NaN total:", sum(is.na(L)), "\n")
# MNAR check: mean observed intensity of proteins with missing vs without
mv <- rowSums(is.na(L)) > 0
miss <- data.frame(n_proteins=nrow(L), n_kept=sum(keep), n_missing_values=sum(is.na(L)),
  n_proteins_with_missing=sum(mv),
  mean_log2_with_missing=mean(rowMeans(L[mv,,drop=FALSE], na.rm=TRUE), na.rm=TRUE),
  mean_log2_without_missing=mean(rowMeans(L[!mv,,drop=FALSE], na.rm=TRUE), na.rm=TRUE))
write.csv(miss, "output/missing_value_summary.csv", row.names=FALSE)
L <- L[keep, , drop=FALSE]; genes <- d$gene[keep]
# median centering
L <- sweep(L, 2, apply(L, 2, median, na.rm=TRUE) - mean(apply(L, 2, median, na.rm=TRUE)))
# MinProb imputation for remaining NAs
for (j in seq_len(ncol(L))) {
  na <- is.na(L[, j]); if (any(na)) {
    q <- quantile(L[, j], 0.01, na.rm=TRUE); s <- sd(L[, j], na.rm=TRUE) * 0.3
    L[na, j] <- rnorm(sum(na), q, s) } }
write.csv(data.frame(protein=rownames(L), gene=genes, L, check.names=FALSE), "output/processed_log2_matrix.csv", row.names=FALSE)
# limma: genotype + run_day (blocking factor, balanced)
g <- factor(m$genotype, levels=c("wildtype","knockout")); day <- factor(m$run_day)
design <- model.matrix(~ g + day)
fit <- eBayes(lmFit(L, design))
tt <- topTable(fit, coef="gknockout", number=Inf, sort.by="none")

  pvalue=tt$P.Value, adjusted_pvalue=tt$adj.P.Val, average_intensity=tt$AveExpr)

}

results.text:
Knockout and wild-type lines differ in the proteome, but the data look unusual, so treat the significance counts with caution. 276 of the 281 proteins that passed filtering have an adjusted p-value below 0.05, and 29 of those also have |log2FC| > 1.

**Method.** I filtered proteins on detection: at least 70% of samples in one genotype. That kept 281 of 300. I log2-transformed and median-centred the intensities. Remaining missing values were imputed with MinProb, since proteins with missing values have lower average intensity, which points to below-detection-limit (MNAR) missingness. I fitted limma with genotype plus run day as a covariate. Run day is balanced across genotypes, so adjusting for it is safe. Adjusted p-values are Benjamini-Hochberg.

**Results** (log2FC is knockout vs wild-type):
- **Up in knockout:** about 27 proteins (P10021, P10026, P10002, P10007 and others) have log2FC ≈ +1.18. A few others reach +0.8 to +2.1.
- **Everything else:** about 247 proteins sit at log2FC ≈ −0.14, essentially constant. That bulk offset is probably a side effect of median normalization, because the shifted proteins pull the median. It is not a real decrease.
- **Reliability:** the −0.14 offset is small, but "significantly down" calls for that bulk are not trustworthy.

**Caveats:**
- **Replicates are not independent.** Within a run day the two lines of the same genotype have nearly identical intensities (KO1≈KO3, KO2≈KO4, and likewise for WT). The gap between the two run days is much larger than the gap between same-day lines. The residual variance is therefore tiny, which makes the p-values (down to ~1e-11) and the 276 significant proteins overconfident. This looks like duplicated or synthetic data, or like a technical effect I can't resolve from the files.
- **Small sample size.** Four lines per genotype is small. Effective independent replication may be closer to two per group.
- I would rank proteins by fold change and validate the ~27 clear up-shifted proteins rather than rely on the p-value threshold.

Not produced: an `.h5ad` of the processed matrix (a required output; only the CSV matrix was written), and the missing-value heatmap, intensity-distribution boxplots, sample-correlation heatmap and protein-coverage plot. The PCA and volcano plots exist. I didn't view either figure.

results.text:
Of 281 proteins tested, 27 are clearly higher in knockout than wild-type, by about 2.5-fold (log2 fold change about 1.3). The other 254 are essentially unchanged. I did not make the AnnData file, the figures or the missing-value summary the protocol asks for.

**How I ran it**
- **Filtering:** I kept proteins detected in at least 3 of 4 lines in either genotype. That kept 281 of 300 proteins, leaving 14 missing values in total.
- **Model:** limma on log2 intensities with genotype and run day as covariates. Missing values were left as they are, with no imputation. Each run day holds two lines of each genotype, so day is not confounded with genotype. P-values are adjusted by Benjamini-Hochberg.
- **Normalization:** I did not normalize. I first tried median centering, but about 10% of proteins are up in knockout, so it dragged the 254 unchanged proteins to a false log2 fold change of about −0.14. Without normalization those proteins sit at about −0.002, so the samples were already on the same scale.

**Results** (`output/de_results_KO_vs_WT.csv`; log2 fold change is knockout over wild-type)
- 27 proteins have a log2 fold change of about 1.3 (about 2.5-fold up).
- 254 proteins have a log2 fold change of about 0.
- The adjusted p-value is below 0.05 for all 281 proteins, including the unchanged ones. Replicate variance is extremely small, so even a −0.002 shift is "significant". This is not evidence of a change. Use the 27 proteins with |log2 fold change| > 1 and an adjusted p-value below 0.05 as the real hits.
- The data look very clean, with two sharply separated groups, almost like simulated data. I cannot say why from the files.

**Caveats**
- With four lines per genotype, treat the 27 hits as solid but the p-values as over-precise.
- I did not check whether any protein IDs are MaxQuant protein groups.

- `output/de_results_KO_vs_WT.csv`
- `output/protein_id_mapping.csv`

results.text:
CATALYST expects marker_class values "type"/"state"/"none"; map them.
Monocytes are the only population that expands after vaccination. They go from 19.6% to 30.3% of cells. Every lymphocyte population shrinks.

I clustered on the 8 lineage markers (arcsinh cofactor 5, FlowSOM, 10 metaclusters). Only 5 metaclusters were non-empty, and each has a clean marker signature. That matches the data being very clean, so I did not tune the clustering further.

| Population | Defining markers | Pre (mean %) | Post (mean %) | log fold change (post/pre) | Adjusted p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CD4 T | CD45+ CD3+ CD4+ | 30.0 | 25.7 | −0.22 | 2e-9 |
| CD8 T | CD45+ CD3+ CD8a+ | 20.0 | 17.7 | −0.18 | 7e-5 |
| NK | CD45+ CD16+ CD56+ | 15.3 | 13.2 | −0.21 | 4e-5 |
| B cells | CD45+ CD19+ | 15.0 | 13.2 | −0.19 | 2e-4 |
| CD14 monocytes | CD45+ CD14+ | 19.6 | 30.3 | +0.62 | 7e-57 |

- **Direction of change:** Frequencies sum to 100% within each sample. The lymphocyte decreases are probably the mathematical consequence of the monocyte increase, not independent losses. Absolute counts would be needed to tell.
- **Functional markers:** I tested pSTAT1, pSTAT3, Ki-67, pERK and Granzyme B within each population. None changed after multiple-testing correction. The smallest adjusted p was 0.33, for Ki-67 in monocytes.
- **Pairing:** The metadata gives different patient IDs for pre (p1–p4) and post (p5–p8). This conflicts with "four donors sampled before and after". The main change after vaccination is that CD14+ monocytes rise from about 19.6% to 30.3% of cells. Every lymphocyte population falls by a smaller amount. The test is unpaired, so this is only suggestive. Pre and post samples carry different patient IDs (p1–p4 versus p5–p8), so the metadata does not link them as the same four donors.

**Method.** I arcsinh-transformed the data (cofactor 5) and clustered on the lineage markers with FlowSOM, using 12 metaclusters. Seven metaclusters contain cells. I labelled them from their median lineage-marker expression, then tested abundance with edgeR on the cluster-by-sample counts.

**Populations and frequencies** (mean of 4 samples per group; `output/DA_results.csv`):

| Population | Pre | Post | log fold change | Adjusted p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CD14+ monocytes | 19.6% | 30.3% | +0.63 | 2.9e-19 |
| CD4 T cells | 30.0% | 25.7% | −0.22 | 3.4e-7 |
| CD8 T cells | 20.0% | 17.7% | −0.18 | 3.4e-4 |
| NK cells (CD16+CD56+) | 15.3% | 13.2% | −0.21 | 3.0e-4 |
| B cells | 15.0% | 13.2% | −0.19 | 8.6e-4 |
| Two ambiguous clusters (4 cells in total) | – | – | – | not interpretable |

**Caveats**
- **Unpaired design:** the test treats the 4 pre and 4 post samples as independent groups, with no donor adjustment.
- **Narrow p-values:** the tiny adjusted p-values come from pooling about 3,000 cells per sample under a count model. They are likely overstated relative to the 4 vs 4 sample comparison.
- **Closed percentages:** the lymphocyte decreases look like the other side of the monocyte rise. Frequencies sum to 100%, so I can't tell a true loss from dilution.
- **Within-sample consistency:** the monocyte increase appears in all four post samples (29–32%) against all four pre samples (19–21%). The lymphocyte shifts are small, a few percentage points.
- **Rare clusters:** clusters 4 and 7 hold 3 and 1 cells, so I left them out of the interpretation.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from cyvcf2 import VCF
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

D = "/analysis-001/data/inputs/f-geno/"
NPC, MAF_MIN, HWE_P, CALL_MIN = 10, 0.01, 1e-6, 0.95

ph = pd.read_csv(D + "pheno.txt", sep="\t")
v = VCF(D + "cohort.vcf.gz")
samples = list(v.samples)
meta, G = [], []
for r in v:
    gt = np.array(r.genotypes)[:, :2]
    g = np.where((gt < 0).any(1), np.nan, gt.sum(1)).astype(float)
    meta.append((r.ID, r.CHROM, r.POS, r.REF, r.ALT[0])); G.append(g)
G = np.array(G).T  # samples x variants
meta = pd.DataFrame(meta, columns=["rsid", "chromosome", "position", "ref", "alt"])
ph = ph.set_index("IID").loc[samples]
y = ph["PHENO1"].values.astype(float)
ok = ~np.isnan(y)
G, y, samples = G[ok], y[ok], np.array(samples)[ok]

# variant QC
call = 1 - np.isnan(G).mean(0)
af = np.nanmean(G, 0) / 2
maf = np.minimum(af, 1 - af)
n = (~np.isnan(G)).sum(0)
p_, q_ = af, 1 - af
obs = np.array([[np.sum(G[:, j] == k) for k in (0, 1, 2)] for j in range(G.shape[1])])
exp = np.stack([n * q_**2, 2 * n * p_ * q_, n * p_**2], 1)
with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    chi = np.nansum((obs - exp) ** 2 / exp, 1)
hwe = stats.chi2.sf(chi, 1)
keep = (call >= CALL_MIN) & (maf >= MAF_MIN) & (hwe > HWE_P)
print("variants kept", keep.sum(), "of", len(keep))

# PCA on standardized, mean-imputed genotypes
Gi = np.where(np.isnan(G), 2 * af, G)
Z = (Gi[:, keep] - 2 * af[keep]) / np.sqrt(2 * af[keep] * (1 - af[keep]))
pcs = PCA(NPC, random_state=0).fit(Z)
PC = pcs.transform(Z)
print("PC var explained", pcs.explained_variance_ratio_[:5])
K = Z @ Z.T / Z.shape[1]
np.fill_diagonal(K, 0)
print("max pairwise kinship-ish", K.max())
pd.DataFrame(PC, index=samples, columns=[f"PC{i+1}" for i in range(NPC)]).assign(LDL=y).to_csv("output/pcs.csv")

# association: OLS with PCs covariates (residualise, then per-variant regression)
C = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), PC])
def resid(a): return a - C @ np.linalg.lstsq(C, a, rcond=None)[0]
yr = resid(y)
res = []
for j in np.where(keep)[0]:
    xr = resid(Gi[:, j])
    sxx = xr @ xr
    b = xr @ yr / sxx
    dof = len(y) - C.shape[1] - 1
    s2 = ((yr - b * xr) ** 2).sum() / dof
    se = np.sqrt(s2 / sxx)
    res.append((j, b, se, 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(b / se), dof)))

Three variants pass Bonferroni correction (p < 1.67e-5 across 2,995 tests) for LDL cholesterol. Two of them also pass the conventional genome-wide threshold of 5e-8. The QQ plot is `figures/qq_plot.png`, with a PDF copy.

| rsid | chr:pos (GRCh38) | beta (mg/dL per alt allele) | SE | p-value | MAF |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| rs100900 | 21:9,975,700 | +13.0 | 1.59 | 1.5e-15 | 0.43 |
| rs100100 | 13:1,997,300 | +12.0 | 2.06 | 8.7e-9 | 0.195 |
| rs101694 | 1:17,894,262 | +12.8 | 3.00 | 2.2e-5 | 0.081 |

- **rs100900 and rs100100:** both pass 5e-8.
- **rs101694:** it passes Bonferroni (p = 2.2e-5) but not 5e-8. Treat it as suggestive.
- **rs102500:** chr15:25,932,500 has p = 5.0e-7, which is suggestive and does not pass Bonferroni.
- **Calibration:** λ_GC is 1.010, so there is no sign of inflation or leftover population structure. The ancestry structure is in the first principal component, which explains 3.8% of variance. The later components each explain about 0.3%.
- **Annotation:** I did not annotate these variants with genes, consequences or gnomAD frequencies. The rsIDs in this VCF are synthetic-looking (`rs100000`, `rs100022`, …), so I would not trust them for database lookups.

**Method.** I ran an ordinary linear regression of LDL on allele dosage in Python (cyvcf2, numpy, scipy), adjusted for 10 genotype principal components. PLINK2 is not installed, so I did not use `--glm`.

**Variant filtering.** The VCF has 3,000 variants and 600 samples, and every variant has FILTER=PASS. I kept variants with call rate ≥ 0.95, MAF ≥ 0.01 and HWE p > 1e-6. That left 2,995 variants. HWE was tested across both ancestries pooled, which can wrongly drop true variants whose frequency differs between ancestries, but only five variants were removed.

**Caveats.**
- **Relatedness:** I checked it only roughly. The largest pairwise kinship-like value is 0.11, below the usual relatedness cutoff of about 0.177, so I excluded no one. This is a rough check, not a formal KING analysis.
- **Variant independence:** the variants were not LD-pruned before the PCA or checked for LD with each other. The three hits are on different chromosomes, so they are probably independent signals.
- **Power:** with 600 samples, the effect sizes of the weaker hits (e.g. rs101694, MAF 0.08) are likely inflated. Replication is needed.

Files are in `/analysis-001/runs/run-001/T1S1`:
- `output/gwas_results.csv`: beta, SE, p-value and MAF for all 2,995 variants
- `output/significant_variants.csv`: the three hits above
- `output/pcs.csv`: the principal components used as covariates
- `figures/qq_plot.png` and `figures/qq_plot.pdf`
- `figures/manhattan.png` and `figures/manhattan.pdf`
- `scripts/gwas.py`
- `logs/gwas.log`

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, cyvcf2, scipy.stats as st
import matplotlib; matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
D="/analysis-001/data/inputs/f-geno/"
NPC=10; MAF_MIN=0.01; MISS_MAX=0.05
ph=pd.read_csv(D+"pheno.txt",sep="\t")
v=cyvcf2.VCF(D+"cohort.vcf.gz"); samples=v.samples
meta=[];G=[]
for r in v:
    g=np.array([ (np.nan if a[0]<0 or a[1]<0 else a[0]+a[1]) for a in r.genotypes],float)
    meta.append((r.ID,r.CHROM,r.POS,r.REF,r.ALT[0],r.FILTER or "PASS")); G.append(g)
G=np.array(G); meta=pd.DataFrame(meta,columns=["rsid","chromosome","position","ref","alt","filter"])
idx=[samples.index(i) for i in ph.IID]; G=G[:,idx]; y=ph.PHENO1.values.astype(float)
print("variants",G.shape, "pheno NA",np.isnan(y).sum())
miss=np.isnan(G).mean(1); af=np.nanmean(G,1)/2; maf=np.minimum(af,1-af)
keep=(miss<=MISS_MAX)&(maf>=MAF_MIN); print("kept",keep.sum())
G=G[keep]; meta=meta[keep].reset_index(drop=True); maf=maf[keep]; af=af[keep]
# impute missing with mean, PCA on standardized genotypes
Gi=np.where(np.isnan(G),np.nanmean(G,1,keepdims=True),G)
Z=(Gi-Gi.mean(1,keepdims=True))/Gi.std(1,keepdims=True)
U,S,Vt=np.linalg.svd(Z,full_matrices=False); pcs=Vt[:NPC].T
pd.DataFrame(pcs,columns=[f"PC{i+1}" for i in range(NPC)]).assign(IID=ph.IID.values).to_csv("output/pcs.csv",index=False)
def gwas(cov):
    X0=np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)),cov]) if cov is not None else np.ones((len(y),1))
    Q,_=np.linalg.qr(X0); yr=y-Q@(Q.T@y); out=[]
    for g in Gi:
        gr=g-Q@(Q.T@g); s=gr@gr
        b=(gr@yr)/s; dof=len(y)-X0.shape[1]-1
        rss=((yr-b*gr)**2).sum(); se=np.sqrt(rss/dof/s)
        out.append((b,se,2*st.t.sf(abs(b/se),dof)))
    return np.array(out)
def lam(p): return np.median(st.chi2.isf(p,1))/st.chi2.isf(0.5,1)
r0=gwas(None); r1=gwas(pcs)
print("lambda no PC",lam(r0[:,2]),"with PCs",lam(r1[:,2]))
res=meta.drop(columns="filter").assign(effect_allele=meta.alt,alt_allele_frequency=af,maf=maf,beta=r1[:,0],standard_error=r1[:,1],pvalue=r1[:,2],pvalue_no_pc_adjustment=r0[:,2])
res=res.sort_values("pvalue"); res.to_csv("output/gwas_results.csv",index=False)
n=len(res); res["bonf"]=res.pvalue*n
sig=res[res.pvalue<0.05/n]; sig.to_csv("output/significant_variants.csv",index=False)
print("Bonferroni threshold",0.05/n,"n sig",len(sig)); print(res.head(15).to_string())
pd.Series({"n_variants":n,"lambda_gc_with_10PCs":lam(r1[:,2]),"lambda_gc_no_PCs":lam(r0[:,2])}).to_csv("output/lambda.csv")
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(10,4.8),sharey=True)
for a,p,t in [(ax[0],r0[:,2],"No covariates"),(ax[1],r1[:,2],f"Adjusted for {NPC} PCs")]:
    o=np.sort(p); e=(np.arange(1,n+1)-0.5)/n
    a.scatter(-np.log10(e),-np.log10(o),s=8,color="#31688e")
    m=max(-np.log10(o).min(),3); a.plot([0,m],[0,m],"k--",lw=1)

PLINK2 isn't installed, so I'll run the regression in Python (numpy/statsmodels) with PCA covariates.
I found three variants associated with LDL cholesterol at the Bonferroni threshold (p < 1.67e-5, which is 0.05 across 3,000 tests). I ran a linear regression for each of the 3,000 variants in 600 people, adjusted for the top 10 genotype principal components. Genotype PCs are needed because the cohort mixes two ancestries.

PLINK2 is not installed, so I ran the regression in Python with numpy and scipy. The model is OLS of LDL on allele dosage plus 10 PCs. All 3,000 variants passed my filters (MAF ≥ 1%, missingness ≤ 5%).

| Variant | Position (GRCh38) | Effect (mg/dL per G allele) | SE | p-value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| rs100900 | chr21:9,975,700 | +13.4 | 1.59 | 2.5e-16 |
| rs100100 | chr13:1,997,300 | +12.7 | 2.02 | 7.4e-10 |
| rs102500 | chr15:25,932,500 | +10.0 | 2.08 | 1.7e-6 |

- **Next best:** rs101694 on chr1 (p = 4.5e-5, beta +12.3) is just short of the threshold. It is suggestive only.
- **Population structure:** Without the PCs, λGC is 3.75, which is severe inflation. With 10 PCs, λGC is 1.013, so the adjusted results look well calibrated.
- **Confounding without PCs:** Without PCs, rs100331, rs101945 and rs100900 look significant (the first two at p ≈ 3e-8 and 1e-7), but rs100331 and rs101945 drop to p = 5.8e-4 and 1.5e-3 once structure is modelled. That fits ancestry confounding. rs100100 and rs102500 only emerge after adjustment.
- **Caveats:** With n = 600, power is limited. Effect sizes of 10–13 mg/dL per allele are very large for real LDL loci, so treat the betas as cohort-specific estimates, not as established effects. The data have no gene annotation, and I did not annotate or do gnomAD lookups. I did not test for relatedness. The 3,000 variants are a sparse set, so a hit marks a region and not a causal variant.

The QQ plot shows unadjusted and PC-adjusted results side by side, with λGC annotated on each panel.
